summary:
## Goal
- Construir agentes duráveis em Node/TypeScript usando `@earendil-works/pi-durable` como biblioteca, no repositório `$HOME/durable.pi`.
- Entender o código do Pi (pi, pi-durable, `pi-ai`, `pi-agent-core`, `pi-coding-agent`, `chord`, `pi-telemetry`, `pi-codemode`, `pi-tui`, `pi-mcp`), verificando API na versão instalada 1.4.0, não de memória.
- Gerenciar contexto como restrição de projeto (AGENTS.md curto, detalhe em `docs/`, âncora em `PROGRESS.md`).
- Operar em time: papéis por quem aprova o quê, SDD com contrato de efeitos, testes de invariante, runbook.
- Definir modelo e protocolo para geração de testes a partir da spec (bake-off), com o modelo vencedor fixado.

## Constraints & Preferences
- Resposta curta, prosa técnica, sem emoji/filler; responder a pergunta antes de agir; dizer se concorda ou discorda antes de listar mudanças.
- Regras de comunicação ficam em `~/.pi/agent/AGENTS.md` (global); `AGENTS.md` do repo não as repete.
- Node 24 (`>=22`), ESM, `module`/`moduleResolution: NodeNext`; sem Bun (decisão explícita).
- `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` ligados; sem `any`, sem `as` para silenciar.
- `AGENTS.md` alvo ~40–50 linhas (hoje 47); procedimento longo vai para `docs/`.
- Tier `contributor` aceito porque o desenvolvimento será open source.
- Não criar extensão de subagentes: usar processo separado `pi --print --no-session`.
- Commit callback puro (só `tx.entry()`/`tx.doc()`), idempotência por chave, determinismo entre checkpoints.

## Progress
### Done
- `AGENTS.md` (47 linhas), `docs/DURABILITY.md`, `docs/PI-CODE-MAP.md`, `NOTES.md`, `docs/RUNBOOK.md`, `specs/_template.md`.
- Configs: `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `eslint.config.js` (ignora `dist/**`, `bakeoff/**`, `test/fixtures/**`; `argsIgnorePattern: "^_"`), `vitest.config.ts`, `src/index.ts`, `.gitignore`.
- `git init` executado; nada commitado (tudo untracked).
- `test/invariants.test.ts` (3): commit atômico, durabilidade em SQLite, commits concorrentes serializam.
- `test/crash.test.ts` (4) + `test/fixtures/effect-child.mjs`: SIGKILL antes/depois da cobrança, resume repetido, provedor idempotente por chave. Teste "tem dentes": remover reconciliação quebra 2 casos.
- `specs/counter/spec.md` + `src/counter.ts` + `test/spec/counter.test.ts` (8 verdes, teste do MiMo adotado).
- `specs/charge/spec.md` + `src/charge.ts` (intenção durável com UUID antes do efeito, resultado no mesmo doc) + `test/spec/charge.test.ts` (9 verdes, teste do Muse ajustado).
- Bake-off generalizado: `scripts/bakeoff.sh <provider/model> [spec]`, fixtures em `bakeoff/fixtures/<spec>/src/`, runs em `bakeoff/runs/<modelo>/<spec>/run-N/`, `summary.txt` com `duration_s` e `wrote_test`.
- `bakeoff/models.txt`: Muse escolhido; MiMo fora; `deepseek-v4.1-flash` como control.
- Gates: `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`, `npm run test` — 24 testes verdes (3 invariante, 8 counter, 9 charge, 4 crash), ~1,6s.

### In Progress
- [ ] Adicionar ao `AGENTS.md` três linhas definindo o modelo de testes (`opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor`), a pasta `test/spec/` e a proibição de editar testes durante a implementação.
- [ ] Adicionar regra do overlay: não devolver valor lido de `tx.doc()` para fora do commit; copiar.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Key Decisions
- **Modelo de testes = `opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor`**: 3/3 runs completam em ~61s e o artefato compila; MiMo V2.6 Flash falhou 3 vezes sem escrever arquivo mesmo com 600s; Minimax falhou 1 de 2 com `TS5097` e variou de 9 para 10 testes.
- **Bake-off mede artefato, não `pi_exit`**: `pi_exit 124` apareceu em run com arquivo completo e compilando; decidem `wrote_test`, `tsc_exit`, citações da spec, `impl_reads`.
- **Protocolo adversarial, não superior**: agente de testes vê só `spec.md`, `AGENTS.md` da fixture e `node_modules` por symlink; tools `read,grep,find,ls,write`; `--thinking low`; máximo 10 testes; import relativo com `.js`; `BACKGROUND_CONTEXT` de `@earendil-works/chord/context`.
- **Runtime Node 24, sem Bun**: invariantes verificados sobre `node:sqlite`; Bun exigiria adaptador `SqliteDatabase` e revalidação.
- **Sem extensão de subagentes**: `pi --print --no-session --model ...` dá isolamento real por processo.
- **`src/counter.ts` usa um único `session.commit`** com `seen: Record<requestId, valor>`: idempotência, concorrência e atomicidade vêm da linha de mutação.
- **`src/charge.ts` grava intenção (com chave UUID) antes do efeito**, depois resultado; provedor idempotente por chave deduplica no replay.

## Next Steps
1. Adicionar as três linhas do modelo de testes e a regra do overlay ao `AGENTS.md`; rodar gates.
2. Crash em processo filho exercitando `chargeOnce` real (hoje o crash usa uma task do fixture).
3. Decidir se `test/spec` vermelho vira gate de CI ou fica manual.
4. Opcional: commit inicial do repositório.
5. Usar o Muse para a próxima spec quando houver novo módulo.

## Critical Context
- Caminhos: `/home/mjabbur/durable.pi/`, docs em `docs/`, specs em `specs/<slug>/spec.md`, testes de contrato em `test/spec/`, fixtures em `bakeoff/fixtures/`.
- Comandos: `npm run typecheck` (`tsc --noEmit`), `npm run test` (`vitest run`), `npm run lint` (`eslint .`); bake-off: `PI_TIMEOUT=600 scripts/bakeoff.sh <provider/model> [spec]`, re-medir com `SCORE_ONLY=1`.
- Erros conhecidos: `TS5097` (import `.ts`), `TS2305` (`BACKGROUND_CONTEXT` não exportado de `@earendil-works/chord`), `TypeError: Cannot use a settled overlay` (retornar valor de `tx.doc()` fora do commit), `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` (rodar `.mjs` fora do repo).
- `ConversationId` é `number` com brand (`idBrand` unique symbol), não `string`.
- Semântica de falha: a chamada que encontra erro de storage rejeita com o **erro original**; chamadas seguintes e waits pendentes rejeitam com `SessionFailed`.
- `restartLimit` default 5 → task `blocked` com `reason: "restart_limit"`; `harness.retryTask(id, ctx)` reexecuta; `harness.closed` com `reason: "failed"` exige reabrir, não retentar `commit`.
- `harness.inspect()` lista só tasks vivas; estado terminal via `getTask(id)`.
- `pi-coding-agent` **não** depende de `pi-durable`; são dois produtos. Duas implementações de compaction, duas noções de `Session`, dois conjuntos de tools.
- Ambiente: `PI_MODEL=deepseek-v4.1-flash`, `PI_PROVIDER=opencode-go`, `PI_REASONING_LEVEL=high`; sessão em `~/.pi/agent/sessions/`.

---

**Turn Context (split turn):**

## Original Request
The user asked (in Portuguese) whether `--thinking` worsens or improves the quality of the tests generated by the Muse model — i.e., does a higher thinking level produce better test output?

## Progress So Far
- Assistant acknowledged there was no existing data: all Muse bake-off runs used `--thinking low`; no higher-level baseline existed. Only latency data was available (MiMo: default level hung >60s on a trivial prompt vs. 14s at `low`), which says nothing about quality.
- Assistant decided to measure directly: same `charge` spec, same contract, different thinking levels.
- Modified `scripts/bakeoff.sh` to parameterize the thinking level: replaced `--thinking low \` with `--thinking "${PI_THINKING:-low}" \`, so the default stays `low`. Verified the change at line 51.
- Ran the bake-off with `PI_THINKING=medium` on model `opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, spec `charge`: wrote_test 1, test_files 1, tests 9, spec_citations 8, src_imports 2, impl_reads 0, tokens unknown.
- Ran with `PI_THINKING=high` on the same model/spec: wrote_test 1, test_files 1, tests 9, spec_citations 8, src_imports 1, impl_reads 0, tokens unknown.
- Inspected existing run summaries under `bakeoff/runs/opencode-go__muse-spark-1.3-contributor/charge/run-{1,2,3}/summary.txt`: duration_s 242 / 61 / 148 respectively, each with `tsc_exit: 0`, `tests: 9`, `spec_citations: 8`.

## Context Needed to Continue
- Repo/working directory: `/home/mjabbur/durable.pi`.
- Bake-off script: `scripts/bakeoff.sh`; now honors `PI_THINKING` env var (default `low`) plus existing `PI_TIMEOUT` (default 240); runs with `pi --print --no-session --model "$MODEL" --thinking ...`.
- Model under test: `opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor`; spec: `charge`.
- Output layout: `bakeoff/runs/<provider>__<model>/<spec>/run-N/summary.txt` containing fields like `duration_s`, `tsc_exit`, `tests`, `spec_citations`.
- Observed so far: medium and high produced identical counts of tests (9) and spec citations (8) versus the prior low runs; only `src_imports` differed (2 at medium, 1 at high) — no quality conclusion drawn yet.
- No token-usage data available (`tokens: ?`), and no wall-clock duration was captured for the new medium/high runs.

sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- codemode: Run JavaScript that calls other tools

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use codemode to batch independent tool calls (Promise.allSettled), chain them, or filter large output, instead of many separate calls.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

<project_instructions path="/home/mjabbur/durable.pi/AGENTS.md">
# AGENTS.md

Node 24, ESM, TypeScript. `@earendil-works/pi-durable` 1.4.0, API experimental:
confira `node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-durable/dist/*.d.ts` antes de usar.
Detalhes em `docs/DURABILITY.md` e `docs/PI-CODE-MAP.md`.

## Comandos

- `npm run typecheck`, `npm run test`, `npm run lint`
- Pronto = os três verdes.

## Durabilidade (não negociável)

- Callback de commit é puro: só `tx.entry()` e `tx.doc()`. Sem I/O, rede, relógio, log.
- Efeito externo só em fase de task: grave intenção + idempotency key, chame,
  grave resultado. No resume, consulte a chave antes de repetir.
- `requestId` estável em todo submit. Entrega é ao menos uma vez.
- Estado é o que foi commitado; memória é cache.
- Determinístico entre checkpoints: `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `process.env`
  e fetch não registrados não entram em prompt nem em decisão.
- `Context` do Chord é por chamada; não guarde nem reuse após settle.
- `defineDoc` sempre com `version`, `history` e `checkpointWhen`.
- Um processo por storage. `MemoryStorage` em teste, SQLite em produção.

## Falhas

- Erro de storage encerra o Harness: escute `harness.closed`, não retente
  `commit`; reabra e reenvie com o mesmo `requestId`.
- `ConversationBusy` e `ReadAfterWrite` são fluxo normal, não bug.
- Todo `await` novo que cruza I/O exige teste de crash (matar e reabrir).

## TypeScript

- `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` ligados.
- Sem `any`; sem `as` para silenciar. Borda externa: `unknown` + schema.
- Tools via `defineTool` (TypeBox). `import type`; ESM com `.js`; sem barrel.

## Código do Pi

Mapa de componentes e ordem de leitura: `docs/PI-CODE-MAP.md`. `rg` pelo símbolo
antes de abrir arquivo. `dist/*.d.ts` é a API real da versão instalada.
Registre achados em `NOTES.md` com `path:linha`, não no chat.

## Escopo

Diff mínimo; sem refatorar fora do pedido; dependência nova: pergunte.
`PROGRESS.md` com estado, decisões e próximos passos.

</project_instructions>
</project_context>

For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

Codemode: `tools.read(args)` resolves to `string | { data: string; mimeType: string; note: string; type: "image"; }`.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description:
Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

Codemode: `tools.bash(args)` resolves to `{ output, truncated, full_output_path?, exit_code, wall_time_seconds }`.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description:
Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

Codemode: `tools.edit(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description:
Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

Codemode: `tools.write(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: codemode
toolsAdded.description:
Run JavaScript that calls other tools. The input is raw JavaScript (not JSON, no code fence), run as an async function body in a QuickJS sandbox: top-level `await` and `return` work. No Node, file system, network, or timers.
- `await tools.<name>({ ...args })` resolves to a string, or an object if the tool's declaration says so, and rejects with an Error on failure. A tool whose declaration returns an object resolves on failure too when it returned that object; check its fields. Calls still running when the script ends are cancelled.
- Optional first line: `// @options: {"max_output_tokens": 10000, "timeout_ms": 60000}`

Globals:
- `text(value)`, `image(dataUrlOrImageBlock)`, `console.log(...)`, and top-level `return` add output; `exit()` ends the script. With several text items, each starts with a `==> text N/M <==` line, and `console` lines follow the other output in one `<console_output>` block. `image()` also saves the image to a temp file and the result names its path.
- `store(key, value)` and `load(key)` keep JSON values across codemode calls.
- `ALL_TOOLS`, `await searchTools(query, { limit?, namespace? })`, `await describeTool(name)`, `await describeNamespace(name)`: find unlisted tools, such as MCP tools.
- `models`: classifiers and image generation. Read /home/mjabbur/.pi/agent/install/releases/1.4.0/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs/codemode.md first.

- Callback de commit é puro: só `tx.entry()` e `tx.doc()`. Sem I/O, rede, relógio, log.

- Todo `await` novo que cruza I/O exige teste de crash (matar e reabrir).

## TypeScript

- `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` ligados.
- Sem `any`; sem `as` para silenciar. Borda externa: `unknown` + schema.

- Callback de commit é puro: só `tx.entry()` e `tx.doc()`. Sem I/O, rede, relógio, log.
- Efeito externo só em fase de task: grave intenção + idempotency key, chame,
  grave resultado. No resume, consulte a chave antes de repetir.
- `requestId` estável em todo submit. Entrega é ao menos uma vez.
- Estado é o que foi commitado; memória é cache.
- Determinístico entre checkpoints: `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `process.env`
  e fetch não registrados não entram em prompt nem em decisão.
- `Context` do Chord é por chamada; não guarde nem reuse após settle.
- `defineDoc` sempre com `version`, `history` e `checkpointWhen`.
- Um processo por storage. `MemoryStorage` em teste, SQLite em produção.
- Valor lido de `tx.doc()` não sai do commit: copie os campos para objeto novo
  (o draft vira overlay e falha depois do settle).

## Testes

- Contrato vem de `specs/`: `test/spec/` é gerado por agente separado
  (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, `--thinking low`), que lê só a spec.
- Não edite `test/spec/` durante a implementação. Teste errado se corrige na
  spec e regenera; o teste não se ajusta ao código.

## Falhas

- Erro de storage encerra o Harness: escute `harness.closed`, não retente
  `commit`; reabra e reenvie com o mesmo `requestId`.
- `ConversationBusy` e `ReadAfterWrite` são fluxo normal, não bug.
- Todo `await` novo que cruza I/O exige teste de crash (matar e reabrir).

## TypeScript

- `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` ligados.
- Sem `any`; sem `as` para silenciar. Borda externa: `unknown` + schema.
- Tools via `defineTool` (TypeBox). `import type`; ESM com `.js`; sem barrel.

## Código do Pi

Mapa e ordem de leitura: `docs/PI-CODE-MAP.md`. `rg` pelo símbolo antes de
abrir arquivo; `dist/*.d.ts` é a API real da versão instalada. Achados vão para
`NOTES.md` com `path:linha`, não para o chat.

## Escopo

Diff mínimo; sem refatorar fora do pedido; dependência nova: pergunte.
`PROGRESS.md` com estado, decisões e próximos passos.

# Mapa do código

Componentes do Pi e do pi-durable, versão 1.4.0. Caminhos relativos a
`node_modules/@earendil-works/<pacote>/dist`. Nenhum pacote publica `src/`;
o `.js` em `dist` é saída do `tsc` com sourcemap, legível.

## 1. Camadas

```
pi-telemetry      contratos de span/métrica, sem dependências
pi-ai             → telemetry, typebox        LLM, providers, Models, streaming
pi-codemode       → quickjs-wasi              sandbox JS com tools injetadas
chord             → telemetry, typebox        Context, plugins, docs, RPC
pi-durable        → chord, pi-ai, pi-codemode, telemetry, typebox, diff, photon
pi-agent-core     → pi-ai, typebox            Agent em memória, sem durabilidade
pi-tui            → marked, ...               render de terminal
pi-mcp            → cross-spawn               cliente MCP
pi-coding-agent   → agent-core, ai, codemode, mcp, tui, ...   CLI/TUI
```

Duas consequências:

- `pi-coding-agent` **não** depende de `pi-durable`. São dois produtos: o CLI usa
  `pi-agent-core` e sessões JSONL próprias; `pi-durable` é biblioteca de harness.
- A seta aponta só para baixo. Precisa de uma tool do coding-agent dentro do
  durable? Copie/adapte; não inverta a dependência.

## 2. pi-durable: conceito → arquivo

| Conceito | Arquivo | Símbolos |
|---|---|---|
| Harness | `harness/harness.d.ts` | `Harness.open`, `DEFAULT_HARNESS_IDENTITY` |
| Tipos centrais | `harness/types.d.ts` | `Harness`, `Conversation`, `Submission`, `Tx`, `Task` |
| Sessão e commits | `session/session.d.ts`, `session/transaction.d.ts` | `createSession`, transação atômica |
| Forks | `session/forks.d.ts` | fork/cópia de conversa |
| Entries | `entries.d.ts` | `UserEntry`, `AssistantEntry`, `ToolResultEntry`, `SystemEntry`, `ResetEntry`, `CompactionEntry`, `defineEntry` |
| Documentos | `documents.d.ts` | `defineDoc`, `defineDocFamily` |
| Tasks | `tasks.d.ts`, `harness/generation.d.ts`, `harness/tool.d.ts` | `defineTask`, `GenerationTask`, `ToolTask` |
| Scheduler e inbox | `harness/scheduler.d.ts`, `harness/inbox.d.ts` | `BlockedReason`, `InboxDoc` |
| Compaction | `harness/compaction.d.ts` | `CompactionTask`, `DEFAULT_COMPACTION_POLICY` |
| Prompt | `harness/prompt.d.ts`, `harness/view.d.ts` | montagem de seções e view da conversa |
| Extensões | `harness/define.d.ts` | `defineExtension`, `defineTool`, `hook`, `section`, `wrapTool` |
| Agent por conversa | `harness/agent.d.ts` | `AgentDoc`, `DEFAULT_RETRY_POLICY`, `DEFAULT_RESTART_LIMIT` |
| Estado vivo | `harness/live.d.ts`, `harness/provider.d.ts`, `harness/usage.d.ts` | `LiveDoc`, `ProviderDoc`, `UsageDoc` |
| Eventos | `harness/events.d.ts` | `watchEvents`, `AgentEvent` |
| Storage | `storage/{memory,sqlite,jsonl,indexeddb}.d.ts` | `MemoryStorage`, `openNodeSqliteStorage`, `openNodeJsonlStorage` |
| Conformidade | `testing/*.d.ts` | `registerStorageConformance` |
| Tools embutidas | `tools/{bash,read,edit,write,image}.d.ts` | implementações próprias |
| Env/sistema | `env/node.d.ts` | filesystem, relógio |
| Code Mode | `codemode/*.d.ts` + pacote `pi-codemode` | integração do sandbox |

## 3. Fluxo de um input

```
submit({ requestId, input })
  → inbox admite e commita           harness/inbox.d.ts
  → pi.generation                    harness/generation.d.ts
      monta prompt                   harness/prompt.d.ts + agent.d.ts
      chama modelo                   pi-ai (Models/stream)
      commita pi.assistant           entries.d.ts
      cria pi.tool × n               harness/tool.d.ts
      espera resultados              harness/scheduler.d.ts
      próxima geração
  → commita resposta final
  → submission settle                harness/submissions.d.ts
```

Os documentos `pi.live` e `pi.inbox` são o estado observável desse fluxo; o
transcript é a verdade.

## 4. Ordem de leitura sugerida

1. `pi-durable/README.md` — conceitos e quick start.
2. `harness/harness.d.ts` e `harness/types.d.ts` — superfície pública.
3. `session/session.d.ts` + `session/transaction.d.ts` — o que é um commit.
4. `documents.d.ts` — documentos, versão, `checkpointWhen`.
5. `tasks.d.ts` → `harness/generation.d.ts` → `harness/tool.d.ts` — o loop.
6. `harness/prompt.d.ts` — como o histórico vira request.
7. `storage/sqlite/*` + `testing/*` — persistência e testes.
8. GitHub, no arquivo `.ts` correspondente, só para o que ainda não fechou.

pi - AI coding assistant with read, bash, edit, write tools

Usage:
  pi [options] [--] [@files...] [messages...]

Commands:
  pi install <source> [-l]     Install extension source and add to settings
  pi remove <source> [-l]      Remove extension source from settings
  pi uninstall <source> [-l]   Alias for remove
  pi update [source|self|pi]   Update pi, extensions, or model catalogs
  pi list                      List installed extensions from settings
  pi config [-l]               Open TUI to enable/disable package resources (Tab switches scope)
  pi auth <command>            Print credentials or check provider readiness
  pi mcp <command>             Check MCP servers, sign in to or out of OAuth servers
  pi <command> --help          Show help for install/remove/uninstall/update/list/config/auth/mcp

Options:
  --provider <name>              Provider to search for --model (requires --model)
  --model <pattern>              Model pattern or ID (supports "provider/id" and optional ":<thinking>")
  --api-key <key>                API key (defaults to env vars)
  --system-prompt <text>         System prompt (default: coding assistant prompt)
  --append-system-prompt <text>  Append text or file contents to the system prompt (can be used multiple times)
  --mode <mode>                  Output mode: text (default), json, or rpc
  --print, -p                    Non-interactive mode: process prompt and exit
  --continue, -c                 Continue previous session
  --resume, -r                   Select a session to resume
  --session <path|id>            Use specific session file or partial UUID
  --session-id <id>              Use exact project session ID, creating it if missing
  --fork <path|id>               Fork specific session file or partial UUID into a new session
  --session-dir <dir>            Directory for session storage and lookup
  --no-session                   Don't save session (ephemeral)
  --name, -n <name>              Set session display name
  --models <patterns>            Comma-separated model patterns for Ctrl+P cycling
                                 Supports globs (anthropic/*, *sonnet*) and fuzzy matching
  --no-tools, -nt                Disable all tools by default (built-in and extension)
  --no-builtin-tools, -nbt       Disable built-in tools by default but keep extension/custom tools enabled
  --tools, -t <tools>            Comma-separated allowlist of tool names or patterns (*) to enable
                                 Keeps MCP tools unless an entry starts with mcp__
                                 Only +name/-name entries add to or remove from the defaults
  --exclude-tools, -xt <tools>   Comma-separated denylist of tool names or patterns (*) to disable
                                 Applies to all tools, MCP tools included
  --thinking <level>             Set thinking level: off, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max
  --extension, -e <path>         Load an extension file or builtin:<name> (can be used multiple times)
  --no-extensions, -ne           Disable extension discovery and built-in extensions (explicit -e paths still work)
  --no-mcp                       Disable built-in MCP support: no servers connect and no MCP tools
  --skill <path>                 Load a skill file or directory (can be used multiple times)

# Marco: Pi durável (CLI e depois web)

Objetivo: um agente de código com o mesmo loop do `pi` — prompt, modelo, tools,
resposta — mas com estado durável. O processo pode morrer em qualquer ponto e a
sessão continua de onde parou, com os mesmos clientes reconectando.

Ordem: CLI primeiro, web depois. A web não é outro agente: é outra vista da
mesma sessão em execução.

## Decisões de arquitetura

**Um dono do storage.** `pi-durable` exige um processo por storage
(`AGENTS.md`, Durabilidade). Logo, o agente roda num processo dono do SQLite e
tanto o CLI quanto o navegador são clientes dele. No M0–M2 o CLI é esse
processo; no M3 ele vira `durable-pi serve` e o CLI passa a anexar por socket.

```
M0–M2:  durable-pi (CLI)  ── dono do SQLite
M3:     durable-pi serve  ── dono do SQLite ── HTTP/WS ──┬── CLI (attach)
                                                        └── browser (Tailscale)
```

**Núcleo separado do cliente desde o primeiro PR.** `src/agent/` monta o
Harness, o registro de tools e a sessão; `src/cli/` só lê argumentos e desenha.
Sem isso, o M3 vira refatoração.

**Um arquivo SQLite por sessão.** `~/.local/share/durable-pi/sessions/<id>.sqlite`.
`--resume` lista arquivos, `--fork` copia, backup é `cp`. Custo: nenhuma consulta
cruzada entre sessões — que não é requisito.

**Streaming é o `watchEvents`.** O evento já traz `snapshot` e deltas de
mensagem (`harness/events.d.ts`). A web usa o mesmo canal; não há protocolo
paralelo para inventar.

## M0 — Fundação: `-p` funcionando

| Passo | Entrega |
|---|---|
| 1 | `src/agent/harness.ts`: `openNodeSqliteStorage` + `Harness.open` com `CodingTools`, `env` apontando para o `cwd`, `root()` com `AgentDoc` (modelo, instruções) |
| 2 | `src/agent/sessions.ts`: caminho, criação, listagem e abertura de sessão |
| 3 | `src/cli/args.ts` + `src/cli/main.ts` + `bin/durable-pi.mjs`: `-p/--print`, `--model`, `--session-dir`, `--no-session` |
| 4 | Teste de integração com provedor fake (`MutableModels.setProvider`): prompt → tool `write` → arquivo existe → transcript persistido |

Aceite: `durable-pi -p "crie hello.txt com olá"` cria o arquivo, imprime a
resposta e deixa sessão em disco. `--continue` na sequência vê o histórico.

## M1 — CLI interativa

- REPL com streaming de texto e de tool slot, indicador de turno em andamento.
- `Ctrl+C` aborta a submission (`abortSubmission`), não o processo.
- `!comando` executa bash direto, fora do modelo.
- Comandos: `/compact`, `/new`, `/resume`, `/model`, `/thinking`, `/usage`.

Aceite: `kill -9` no meio de uma geração; ao reabrir, a submission pendente
termina e o transcript não tem tool call duplicada.

## M2 — Paridade durável com o CLI atual

| Recurso do `pi` | Como entra |
|---|---|
| `--continue`, `--resume`, `--fork`, `--session`, `--name` | sessões em arquivo (M0) + `fork(at)` |
| compactação automática | `DEFAULT_COMPACTION_POLICY` do Harness |
| retry e restart limit | `settings` do Harness, com `/retry` para task parkada |
| `AGENTS.md` do projeto | descoberta no `cwd` → `AgentDoc.instructions` |
| `--thinking`, `--tools`, `--exclude-tools` | `AgentChange` + allowlist no registro |
| `--print --mode json` | serialização dos eventos, sem TUI |

Aceite: paridade funcional nos cinco cenários do runbook, incluindo crash
durante `bash` (efeito já commitado não reexecuta) e fork a partir de entrada
antiga.

## M3 — Servidor e interface web

| Passo | Entrega |
|---|---|
| 1 | `durable-pi serve --session <id> --port 8787`, bind em `127.0.0.1` |
| 2 | API: `GET /api/sessions`, `GET /api/sessions/:id/context`, `WS /api/sessions/:id/events`, `POST submit|abort|compact` |
| 3 | SPA mobile-first: transcript, composer, stop, estado da conexão, reconexão por snapshot |
| 4 | `tailscale serve --bg --https=443 http://127.0.0.1:8787`, auth por token + identidade da tailnet |

Aceite: no celular, pela tailnet, enviar prompt e ver streaming; derrubar o
daemon no meio e reabrir — a sessão continua e o cliente re-sincroniza sozinho.
Dois clientes abertos veem o mesmo transcript.

Autenticação: token em `~/.config/durable-pi/token` e allowlist de logins da
tailnet. Sem cadastro de usuário no v1. Nunca bind em `0.0.0.0`.

## M4 — Resto da paridade

MCP, skills, prompt templates, code mode, subagentes, `--mode rpc`, export
HTML. Cada um é PR próprio, sem bloquear o marco.

## Fora de escopo no v1

TUI fullscreen com widgets, temas, `pi install`/marketplace, terminal setup e
UI de extensões. São conforto, não durabilidade.

## Riscos e decisões abertas

1. **TUI própria ou `pi-tui`.** `pi-tui` não é dependência deste repositório;
   adicionar é dependência nova. Proposta: ANSI próprio no M1, reavaliar no M2.
2. **Credenciais de modelo.** `createModels()` não lê a configuração do `pi`.
   Precisamos de `~/.config/durable-pi/models.json` e das env vars usuais;
   reusar `~/.pi/agent/auth.json` exige decisão explícita.
3. **Permissão de tool.** `bash` roda sem sandbox. No v1: allowlist de comandos
   e `cwd` fixo, com o risco documentado no runbook.
4. **Dois clientes submetendo ao mesmo tempo.** O servidor serializa; o segundo
   recebe `ConversationBusy`, que é fluxo normal e vira mensagem na UI.

## Ordem de trabalho

M0 (2 PRs) → M1 (2 PRs) → M2 (3 PRs) → M3 (4 PRs). Cada PR com os três gates
verdes; crash test obrigatório em todo passo que cruza I/O novo.

## Definição de pronto do marco

CLI instalável rodando o loop completo com sessão durável, servidor web
acessível pela tailnet no celular, crash tests cobrindo geração e tool call, e
`README` com quickstart de CLI e de web.

content.text: # Run Pi safely Treat model-generated commands and code as untrusted. Pi can read, change, and execute files with the permissions of the account that started it, and it does not ask for approval before every tool call. Extensions, package installers, language servers, and other child processes run with those same permissions unless an operating-system or virtualization boundary restricts them. Files, comments, instructions, command output, and model responses can steer the model through prompt injection. Project trust controls which project resources load at startup, but it does not make that content or the resulting actions safe. Safety comes from limiting the files, credentials, processes, and network services Pi can access and affect if a generated action is wrong or hostile. Watching the transcript, using project trust, and reviewing changes do not create a security boundary. ## Choose how to run Pi Different ways of running Pi place different limits on what generated commands can access: | How Pi runs | What remains protected | |---|---| | Directly, with the permissions of its operating-system user | Anything that user cannot access. A dedicated user account can narrow those permissions, but Pi still shares the operating system and network with other users. | | Entirely inside a container, virtual machine, or sandbox | Host files and processes that you do not expose to the environment. Credentials and network services remain accessible if you make them available inside it. This is usually the strongest practical option. | | Outside the isolated environment, with only its built-in tools running inside | Host resources are protected from actions performed through those tools. Pi itself and other extensions remain outside the boundary, so this is a narrower form of isolation. | The working folder controls resource discovery and the default location for tools, but it does not prevent commands from accessing other paths available to the Pi process. Whichever option you choose, only provide the files and services required for the task. Keep credentials outside the environment where possible, or use narrowly scoped, short-lived credentials. Restrict network access when commands do not need it. For setup instructions and the limitations of each isolation method, see [Run Pi in an isolated environment](containerization.md). ## Understand project trust Project trust controls whether Pi loads most settings and resources supplied by a working folder. It prevents a folder from silently loading executable extensions before you approve it. Project trust is not a complete startup boundary. Pi reads the project `sessionDir` setting while selecting or creating a session, before it resolves project trust. Declining trust prevents the remaining project settings and protected resources from loading, but it cannot undo that initial session-directory lookup. Project trust does not limit what tool calls can access or affect. After Pi starts, enabled tools still use the operating-system permissions of the Pi process. Instructions and other content in the folder can also influence the model. ### Resources protected by project trust Pi requires a project-trust decision when it finds any of these resources from the current working directory: - `.pi/settings.json` - `.pi/mcp.json` === containerization === # Run Pi in an isolated environment Use an isolated environment to limit the files, credentials, processes, and network services that generated commands can access or affect. You can isolate the complete Pi process or keep Pi on the host and route selected tools into an isolated environment. ## Choose an isolation method | Method | Where Pi runs | What is isolated | Credential handling | Best for | |---|---|---|---|---| | Plain Docker | Container | Pi, built-in tools, `!` commands, and extensions | Credentials passed into the container | A straightforward local container boundary | | Docker Sandboxes | Managed sandbox | Pi, built-in tools, `!` commands, and extensions | Provider credentials remain on the host and are substituted by the proxy | Managed local isolation without exposing the real provider key | | OpenShell | Local or remote sandbox | Pi, built-in tools, `!` commands, and extensions | Policy-controlled credentials and inference routing | Filesystem, process, network, and credential policies | | Gondolin extension | Host | Built-in tools and `!` commands | Stored Pi credentials remain on the host, but commands inherit host environment variables | A local micro-VM for tool execution while retaining the host interface | The method changes where extensions run. When the complete Pi process runs inside an isolated environment, its extensions run there too. When host Pi delegates built-in tools through Gondolin, other extension tools still run on the host unless they also delegate their work. ## Decide what Pi can access An isolated process can still affect resources you expose to it: - A read-write host mount lets Pi modify those host files. - Mounting `~/.pi/agent` exposes your Pi credentials, settings, extensions, and sessions. - Environment variables passed into a container are available to processes inside it. - Network access may allow code or tool output to leave the environment. - Tool-only isolation does not constrain the host Pi process or extension tools that do not use the isolated backend. Expose only the working folder, credentials, and network destinations needed for the task. Use read-only mounts or copy files into and out of the environment when you do not want writes to affect the host. ## Run Pi in plain Docker

## Run Pi in plain Docker

Plain Docker provides the simplest whole-process container boundary.

### Build the image

Create `Dockerfile.pi`:

```dockerfile
FROM node:24-bookworm-slim

RUN apt-get update \
  && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends bash ca-certificates git ripgrep \
  && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN npm install -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent

WORKDIR /workspace
ENTRYPOINT ["pi"]
```

Build it from the directory containing the file:

```bash
docker build -t pi-sandbox -f Dockerfile.pi .
```

### Start Pi

From the working folder you want Pi to access, run:

```bash
docker run --rm -it \
  -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace" \
  -v pi-agent-home:/root/.pi/agent \
  pi-sandbox
```

Replace `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` with the credential required by your provider. The named `pi-agent-home` volume keeps container-local settings, credentials, and sessions between runs.

Do not mount the host's `~/.pi/agent` unless the container should have access to your host Pi configuration and credentials.

### Verify the workspace

Inside Pi, run:

```text
!pwd
```

The command should report `/workspace`. Changes under `/workspace` write through to the mounted host folder. Remove the bind mount or use a read-only mount when that is not acceptable.

## Run Pi with Docker Sandboxes

[Docker Sandboxes](https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/) runs the complete Pi process inside a managed sandbox. Its proxy can keep the real provider credential on the host and substitute it when requests leave the sandbox.

Configure credentials before creating the sandbox. Do not run `/login` inside the sandbox because that writes a real credential into it.

### Use a Claude Pro or Max token

Generate the token with `claude setup-token` on a machine with Claude Code. If an `anthropic` secret is already configured, remove it first so the proxy does not add an API-key header alongside the bearer token:

```bash
sbx secret rm anthropic

sbx secret set-custom \
  --host api.anthropic.com \
  --env ANTHROPIC_OAUTH_TOKEN \
  --placeholder 'sk-ant-oat01-{rand}'
```

`sbx secret set-custom` reads the real token from standard input. The sandbox receives an OAuth-shaped placeholder, which the proxy replaces only for requests to the configured host.

For an Anthropic API key, use `sbx secret set anthropic` instead.

### Start Pi

Run this from the working folder you want mounted:

```bash
sbx run --kit "docker.io/sbx/pi-kit:latest" pi
```

For an existing sandbox, run Pi non-interactively with:

```bash
sbx exec <sandbox-name> -- pi -p "list the failing tests"
```

See the [Pi kit documentation](https://github.com/docker/sbx-kits-contrib/tree/main/pi) for other providers, troubleshooting, and image pinning.

# Marco: Pi durável (CLI e depois web)

Objetivo: um agente de código com o mesmo loop do `pi` — prompt, modelo, tools,
resposta — mas com estado durável. O processo pode morrer em qualquer ponto e a
sessão continua de onde parou, com os mesmos clientes reconectando.

Ordem: CLI primeiro, web depois. A web não é outro agente: é outra vista da
mesma sessão em execução. A meta de interface é paridade com o `pi-ui`,
acompanhando o desenvolvimento dele.

## Decisões de arquitetura

**Um dono do storage.** `pi-durable` exige um processo por storage
(`AGENTS.md`, Durabilidade). Logo, o agente roda num processo dono do SQLite e
tanto o CLI quanto o navegador são clientes dele. No M0–M2 o CLI é esse
processo; no M3 ele vira `durable-pi serve` e o CLI passa a anexar por socket.

```
M0–M2:  durable-pi (CLI)  ── dono do SQLite
M3:     durable-pi serve  ── dono do SQLite ── HTTP/WS ──┬── CLI (attach)
                                                        └── browser (Tailscale)
```

**Núcleo separado do cliente desde o primeiro PR.** `src/agent/` monta o
Harness, o registro de tools e a sessão; `src/cli/` só lê argumentos e desenha.
Sem isso, o M3 vira refatoração.

**Tudo roda em container, CLI incluído.** O container é a fronteira de
segurança; o host só roda Docker e Tailscale. O agente executa comandos
arbitrários com permissões de usuário, e o `pi` não finge ter sandbox
(`docs/security.md`): isolamento é do ambiente. Consequências aceitas: o
workspace entra por bind rw, o SQLite fica em volume nomeado (locking quebra em
filesystem de rede) e credencial de provedor entra por env, nunca por mount de
`~/.pi`.

**Distribuição é imagem.** Não há instalação global no host. O CLI é
`docker run -it` com o `cwd` montado em `/workspace`.

**Um arquivo SQLite por sessão**, dentro do volume:
`/home/agent/.local/share/durable-pi/sessions/<id>.sqlite`. `--resume` lista
arquivos, `--fork` copia, backup é copiar do volume.

**TUI é `pi-tui`.** `@earendil-works/pi-tui` 1.4.0, MIT, sem dependência de
`pi-agent-core`. A TUI é um adaptador: `watchEvents` → entradas do transcript →
`Markdown`, `ScrollView`, `Editor`, `SelectList`. Versão exata fixada.

**Streaming é o `watchEvents`.** O evento já traz `snapshot` e deltas de
mensagem (`harness/events.d.ts`). A web usa o mesmo canal; não há protocolo
paralelo para inventar.

## M0 — Fundação: `-p` funcionando

| Passo | Entrega |
|---|---|
| 1 | `src/agent/harness.ts`: `openNodeSqliteStorage` + `Harness.open` com `CodingTools`, `env` apontando para `/workspace`, `root()` com `AgentDoc` (modelo, instruções) |
| 2 | `src/agent/sessions.ts`: caminho, criação, listagem e abertura de sessão |
| 3 | `src/cli/args.ts` + `src/cli/main.ts` + `bin/durable-pi.mjs`: `-p/--print`, `--model`, `--session-dir`, `--no-session` |
| 4 | `Dockerfile` (node 24-slim + git, ripgrep, bash), `scripts/run.sh` que monta `cwd` e o volume |
| 5 | Teste de integração com provedor fake (`MutableModels.setProvider`): prompt → tool `write` → arquivo existe → transcript persistido |

Aceite: `scripts/run.sh -p "crie hello.txt com olá"` cria o arquivo no `cwd`,
imprime a resposta e deixa sessão no volume. `--continue` na sequência vê o
histórico.

Testes e gates continuam rodando no host; o container é para executar o agente,
não para desenvolver este repositório.

## M1 — CLI interativa

- TUI sobre `pi-tui`: transcript com markdown, streaming de texto e de tool
  slot, editor com histórico, status de turno.
- `Ctrl+C` aborta a submission (`abortSubmission`), não o processo.
- `!comando` executa bash direto, fora do modelo.
- Comandos: `/compact`, `/new`, `/resume`, `/model`, `/thinking`, `/usage`.

Aceite: `kill -9` no container durante uma geração; ao reabrir, a submission
pendente termina e o transcript não tem tool call duplicada.

## M2 — Paridade durável com o CLI atual

| Recurso do `pi` | Como entra |
|---|---|
| `--continue`, `--resume`, `--fork`, `--session`, `--name` | sessões em arquivo (M0) + `fork(at)` |
| compactação automática | `DEFAULT_COMPACTION_POLICY` do Harness |
| retry e restart limit | `settings` do Harness, com `/retry` para task parkada |
| `AGENTS.md` do projeto | descoberta no `/workspace` → `AgentDoc.instructions` |
| `--thinking`, `--tools`, `--exclude-tools` | `AgentChange` + allowlist no registro |
| `--print --mode json` | serialização dos eventos, sem TUI |

Aceite: paridade funcional nos cinco cenários do runbook, incluindo crash
durante `bash` (efeito já commitado não reexecuta) e fork a partir de entrada
antiga.

## M3 — Servidor e interface web

| Passo | Entrega |
|---|---|
| 1 | `durable-pi serve --session <id> --port 8787` dentro do container, bind em `127.0.0.1` |
| 2 | API: `GET /api/sessions`, `GET /api/sessions/:id/context`, `WS /api/sessions/:id/events`, `POST submit|abort|compact` |
| 3 | SPA mobile-first: transcript, composer, stop, estado da conexão, reconexão por snapshot |
| 4 | porta publicada em `127.0.0.1:8787` no host; `tailscale serve --bg --https=443 http://127.0.0.1:8787` na frente |

Aceite: no celular, pela tailnet, enviar prompt e ver streaming; derrubar o
container no meio e subir de novo — a sessão continua e o cliente
re-sincroniza sozinho. Dois clientes abertos veem o mesmo transcript.

Autenticação: token em `~/.config/durable-pi/token` e allowlist de logins da
tailnet. Sem cadastro de usuário no v1. O container nunca bind em `0.0.0.0`
exposto à tailnet.

## M4 — Resto da paridade

MCP, skills, prompt templates, code mode, subagentes, `--mode rpc`, export
HTML. Cada um é PR próprio, sem bloquear o marco.

## Fora de escopo no v1

Temas, `pi install`/marketplace, terminal setup e UI de extensões. São conforto,
não durabilidade.

## Riscos e decisões abertas

1. **Credenciais de `git` dentro do container.** `git push` exige token ou
   agente SSH montado; o mount do socket `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` reduz o isolamento.
   Decidir no M1: token por env ou nada (commits locais apenas).
2. **Credenciais de modelo.** `createModels()` não lê a configuração do `pi`.
   `~/.config/durable-pi/models.json` no volume + env vars usuais; reusar
   `~/.pi/agent/auth.json` está descartado.
3. **`bash` sem sandbox dentro do container.** Allowlist de comandos e `cwd`
   fixo são higiene, não fronteira; a fronteira é o container. Documentar no
   runbook o que o bind do workspace expõe.
4. **Dois clientes submetendo ao mesmo tempo.** O servidor serializa; o segundo
   recebe `ConversationBusy`, que é fluxo normal e vira mensagem na UI.
5. **`pi-tui` em TTY de container.** Verificar resize, clipboard nativo e
   mouse no M1; o pacote traz prebuilds por plataforma.

## Ordem de trabalho

M0 (3 PRs: núcleo, CLI+Dockerfile, integração) → M1 (2 PRs) → M2 (3 PRs) → M3
(4 PRs). Cada PR com os três gates verdes; crash test obrigatório em todo passo
que cruza I/O novo.

## Definição de pronto do marco

Imagem construível rodando o loop completo com sessão durável, servidor web
acessível pela tailnet no celular, crash tests cobrindo geração e tool call, e
`README` com quickstart de CLI e de web via `docker run`.

# @earendil-works/pi-durable

> **Experimental.** The API changes without notice between releases.

A durable agent harness. Conversations, model turns, tool calls, and your own state are committed to storage before anything is shown. If the process dies mid-turn, reopening the storage picks the work up where it stopped.

Built on [`@earendil-works/pi-ai`](../ai/README.md) for model access and `@earendil-works/chord` for document state.

## Table of Contents

- [Installation](#installation)
- [Quick Start](#quick-start)
- [Concepts](#concepts)
- [Persist and Resume](#persist-and-resume)
- [Extensions](#extensions)
- [Tools](#tools)
- [Code Mode](#code-mode)
- [System Prompt](#system-prompt)
- [Per-Conversation Agent](#per-conversation-agent)
- [Settings](#settings)
- [Environment](#environment)
- [Reload](#reload)
- [Watching a Conversation](#watching-a-conversation)
- [Busy Conversations](#busy-conversations)
- [Reset and Handoff](#reset-and-handoff)
- [Compaction](#compaction)
- [Agent Events (Experimental)](#agent-events-experimental)
- [Hooks](#hooks)
- [More Conversations and Forks](#more-conversations-and-forks)
- [Abort and Subagents](#abort-and-subagents)
- [Child Tasks](#child-tasks)
- [Task Graph](#task-graph)
- [Your Own State](#your-own-state)
- [Usage and Cost](#usage-and-cost)
- [Storage](#storage)
- [Errors](#errors)
- [Examples](#examples)
- [Design Documents](#design-documents)

## Installation

```bash
npm install @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/chord
```

## Quick Start

```typescript
import { BACKGROUND_CONTEXT } from "@earendil-works/chord/context";
import { createModels } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/models";
import { openaiProvider } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/providers/openai";
import { AssistantEntry, createRegistry, Harness, MemoryStorage } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable";

const context = BACKGROUND_CONTEXT;

const models = createModels();
models.setProvider(openaiProvider()); // reads OPENAI_API_KEY

const harness = await Harness.open(new MemoryStorage(), { models, registry: createRegistry() }, context);
const root = await harness.root(context, { agent: { model: { provider: "openai", modelId: "gpt-6-sol" } } });

const submission = await root.submit({ type: "input", content: "What is the capital of France?" }, context);
const settled = await submission.wait(context);
if (settled.status === "done" && settled.type === "input") {
	const answer = await root.commit((tx) => tx.entry(AssistantEntry, settled.answer), context);
	console.log(answer?.model?.[0]);
}
await harness.close(context);
```

What happened:

- `Harness.open()` opens a Session over a storage backend. `MemoryStorage` keeps everything in memory.
- `root()` returns the root conversation, creating it on first use with the given agent choices. A conversation is a transcript of immutable entries.
- `submit()` durably admits your input and returns a `Submission`. A built-in generation task calls the model and appends the answer.
- `wait()` resolves once the input is answered (`done`) or has failed (`unanswered`, with a reason).

Every async call takes a Chord `Context`, which carries cancellation and its current `TelemetrySpan`. `BACKGROUND_CONTEXT` never cancels and uses a NOOP span. The Harness owns the root adapter; adapters are never stored in a `Context`. Cancelling a wait only cancels that wait, never the work.

`HarnessOptions.identity` sets how model requests identify the app to providers (a pi-ai `ClientIdentity`), merged over `DEFAULT_HARNESS_IDENTITY` (`{ attribution: PI_ATTRIBUTION }`: OpenRouter, NVIDIA NIM, and OpenCode attribution headers name pi). It applies to generation, compaction, hooks, and tools, over the identity the host's `Models` was created with. Pass your app's attribution, for example `{ attribution: { name: "my-app", url: "https://my-app.example" } }`, or `{ attribution: null }` to send none.

`HarnessOptions.telemetry` accepts a host-owned `TelemetryContext` from `@earendil-works/pi-telemetry`, with optional `propagation` and `metrics` capabilities; omitted, it is a no-op. `DURABLE_TELEMETRY_SCHEMA`, exported from the package root, documents its typed spans, events, and metrics. Attributes contain IDs and control metadata, never messages, arguments, or results; IDs point to the transcript.

- `pi.durable.submit` covers the public submit call and its commit. Each input starts a new root trace with a link to its caller's current span; a write is a child of its caller. Duplicate `requestId` preserves the original submission and carrier. Internal admissions, such as compaction writes, emit events on their phase span without a submit span.
- `pi.durable.phase` covers one run or abort phase of every task, including its decision commit, never the next phase, a durable wait, or a restart. Its attributes identify the task, phase, attempt when present, `resumed`, and outcome. Tool phases also identify the tool and call. Nested tasks and background compactions inherit the creating phase; model requests receive that phase context. Hooks add no spans.
- Failed phase outcomes set error status with a fixed category (`task_faulted`, `task_failed`, or `task_orphaned`) and the outcome's diagnostic message, truncated to 500 characters (the reason for an orphaned task). Diagnostics can contain caller content; no error detail or exception name is recorded. An `aborted` outcome keeps status `ok`, including interruption by close or cancellation.
- Every `onReport` report also emits a `pi.durable.report` event on its current span. Without a span, the NOOP span drops the event; no root report span is created. Only `type`, optional fixed `reason`, `extension`, and `task.id` are recorded; no error payload is included. `pi.durable.reports` counts all reports by `type` only, including those without a span. Clock failures report without a phase context. The `onReport` callback is unchanged.
- Committed entries and settled submissions emit `pi.durable.entry` and `pi.durable.submission`. Committed running phase changes emit `pi.durable.checkpoint`; a nested call answered from its stored result emits `pi.durable.replay`.
- Propagation stores optional opaque `trace` carriers in submission and task JSON without a storage migration. Phase spans extract their task's stored carrier, or start at the adapter root when absent or unknown. `TaskOptions.trace` inherits the creator's carrier when absent, accepts an explicit carrier override, or uses `"root"` to start at the adapter root without storing a carrier. A run started for several queued inputs takes the first input's trace; its first invocation's phase spans link to the other inputs through immutable task `links`. A steer stays in the running trace and its submit span links to that run's stored carrier. A reopened task's first invocation has `resumed: true` in the same trace.
- Metrics record `pi.durable.phase.duration` (milliseconds; task, phase, outcome) and `pi.durable.tasks.active` (live tasks; task name), without record IDs. Closing the Harness releases its active counts.

## Concepts

- **Harness**: one open storage plus the machinery that runs agents on it. All changes go through one line of atomic commits, and nothing is shown before its commit is stored.
- **Conversation**: a transcript. `root()` creates the root conversation on first use; you can create more and fork them. A `Conversation` handle holds no state; compare handles by `id`.
- **Entry**: one immutable transcript record, such as a user message (`pi.user`), a model response (`pi.assistant`), a tool result (`pi.tool-result`), a system prompt change (`pi.system`), a reset (`pi.reset`), or your own kind. The model sees the entries from the newest reset onward.
- **Commit**: an atomic write. `conversation.commit((tx) => ...)` can append entries, edit documents, and create tasks together; either all of it is stored or none of it.
- **Document**: typed JSON state stored next to the transcript and changed in commits. Built-in ones hold each conversation's agent choices (`pi.agent`), provider-facing session identity (`pi.provider`), running generation and tools (`pi.live`), queued submissions (`pi.inbox`), and spend (`pi.usage`).
- **Task**: a durable state machine that saves a checkpoint at every step, so a restarted process continues from the last one. Every task has an owner: its conversation, or another task. The Harness runs answers as built-in tasks: `pi.generation` calls the model and owns the `pi.tool` tasks of its tool calls, waits for them, and hands the run to the next generation.
- **Submission**: something you hand to a conversation, either user input or an entry to write, which you can wait for.
- **Turn and run**: a turn is one model response and its tool calls; a run is the turns from an input to its final answer. A conversation is busy while a run is going.
- **Extension**: a named bundle of tools, system prompt sections, hooks, wrappers, and tasks.
- **Registry**: the extensions this process installed. It can change while the Harness runs; new work uses the new state.
- **Agent**: what a conversation runs with: model, thinking level, selected extensions, tools, instructions, and working directory. Stored per conversation as names in `pi.agent`, resolved against the registry at each use.

One answered input, as entries and tasks:

```text
submit(input) → pi.user
  pi.generation → pi.system (only if the prompt or tools changed), pi.assistant (tool calls)
    pi.tool × n → pi.tool-result × n   (owned by the generation, which waits for them)
  pi.generation → pi.assistant (answer) → submission done
```

Use SQLite or JSONL storage to keep conversations across restarts:

# WSL container

The WSL container feature has two major components: a CLI called `wslc.exe` to build, run and interact with Linux containers and a WSL container API allowing Windows app developers to use Linux containers as part of their app logic. 

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The WSL container feature requires **WSL version 2.9.3 or higher**. To update to the latest version, open PowerShell and enter:
>
> ```powershell
> wsl --update
> ```
>
> Check your installed version at any time with `wsl --version`.

## WSL container CLI

WSL now includes `wslc.exe` as a built in binary. Its goal is to have a familiar CLI interface, allowing you to easily build, run and interact with Linux containers. 

See some of the example commands below:

```powershell
# Run a container
wslc run --rm -it ubuntu:latest bash -c "echo Hello world from WSL container!"
# List available images
wslc image ls
# Run a web server
wslc run -it --rm -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx
# Get its content
curl localhost:8080
# List the container
wslc container ps
# Stop the container
wslc container stop web
```

You can learn more on how to get started with this feature at [our container tutorial](./tutorials/wsl-containers.md).

To configure resources and other options for `wslc.exe`, such as CPU count, memory, and storage location, see [WSL container settings](./wsl-container-settings.md).

## WSL container API

Windows applications can make use of Linux containers as well! The WSL container API NuGet package allows you to programmatically pull, run, and interact with Linux containers, including key interactions like stdin and stdout, file mounts, networking mounts, GPU access and more.

For the complete API surface across the C, C#, and C++ projections, see the [WSL container API reference](https://wsl.dev/api-reference/).

### Install the API

The WSL container API ships in the `Microsoft.WSL.Containers` NuGet package, which provides both the C# projection and the C++/WinRT headers.

# [C#](#tab/csharp)

Add the package to your project with the .NET CLI:

```powershell
dotnet add package Microsoft.WSL.Containers
```

Then import the namespace in your code:

```csharp
using Microsoft.WSL.Containers;
```

# [C++](#tab/cpp)

Add the `Microsoft.WSL.Containers` NuGet package to your C++/WinRT project, then include the projected header and bring the namespace into scope:

```cpp
#include <winrt/Microsoft.WSL.Containers.h>

using namespace winrt::Microsoft::WSL::Containers;
```

> [!NOTE]
> The C++/WinRT projection is in preview and is subject to breaking changes.

---

### API overview

The API is organized around a small set of objects that mirror the lifecycle of running a container:

| Object | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `WslcService` | Static entry point for service-level operations. Use it to check that the required WSL components are installed, query the service version, and install missing dependencies. |
| `Session` | A WSL-backed host that runs your containers. A session manages images (pull, import, load, push, tag, delete) and creates containers. |
| `Container` | A container created inside a session. Use it to start, stop, inspect, and delete the container, and to run additional processes inside it. |
| `Process` | A Linux process running in a container. Use it to read `stdout`/`stderr`, write to `stdin`, send signals, and observe exit codes through events. |

A typical flow is: verify prerequisites with `WslcService`, create and start a `Session`, pull an image, configure and create a `Container`, then start it and interact with its `Process` objects.

The snippets below show the same core building blocks in each supported language. Use the tabs to switch between C# and C++.

**Check that the required components are installed:**

```csharp

if (missing != ComponentFlags.None)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"WSL components are missing ({missing}). Run: wsl --install");
    return;
}
```

# Get started with WSL container

This step-by-step guide will help you get started building and running Linux containers on Windows using **`wslc.exe`**, the container CLI that ships built in with WSL. 

`wslc.exe` provides a familiar CLI for building, shipping, and running containerized apps.

## Overview of WSL containers

A container is a tool used to create, deploy, and run applications. Containers enable developers to package an app with all of the parts it needs (libraries, frameworks, dependencies, etc) and ship it all out as one package. Using a container ensures that the app will run the same regardless of any customized settings or previously installed libraries on the computer running it that could differ from the machine that was used to write and test the app's code. This permits developers to focus on writing code without worrying about the system that code will be run on.

## Prerequisites

- WSL installed, version 2.9.3 or higher. Run `wsl --update` to get the latest version.
- [Install Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) *(optional)*. This will provide the best experience, including the ability to code and debug your containerized projects connected to your Linux distribution.
- [Install Windows Terminal](/windows/terminal/get-started) *(optional)*. This will provide the best experience, including the ability to customize and open multiple terminals in the same interface (including Ubuntu, Debian, PowerShell, Azure CLI, or whatever you prefer to use).

## Install and verify wslc

`wslc.exe` is included with WSL, so there's no separate engine to install. It requires WSL version 2.9.3 or higher. To make sure you have a version of WSL that includes it:

1. [Install WSL](../install.md) if you haven't already, then update to the latest version by opening PowerShell and entering:

    ```powershell
    wsl --update
    ```

    > [!NOTE]
    > WSL container requires WSL version 2.9.3 or higher. You can confirm your WSL version with `wsl --version`.

2. Confirm that `wslc.exe` is available and check its version by entering:

    ```powershell
    wslc version
    ```

3. Test that everything works correctly by running a simple built-in image. The image is automatically pulled if it isn't already present locally:

    ```powershell
    wslc run --rm hello-world
    ```

    You should see a "Hello" message confirming that your installation appears to be working correctly.

> [!TIP]
> Here are a few helpful `wslc` commands to know:
>
> - List the commands available in the `wslc` CLI by entering: `wslc --help`
> - List information for a specific command with: `wslc <COMMAND> --help`
> - List the images on your machine, with: `wslc image list`
> - List the running containers on your machine, with: `wslc container list` or list all containers (including stopped ones) with: `wslc container list --all`
> - Display resource usage statistics for your running containers, with: `wslc stats`

## Run your first containers

With `wslc.exe` you can pull images, run containers in the foreground or background, publish ports, and interact with running containers. Try a few of these commands from PowerShell:

```powershell
# Run a command in a throwaway container
wslc run --rm -it ubuntu:latest bash -c "echo Hello world from WSL container!"

# Run a web server in the background and publish port 8080 to the container's port 80
wslc run -d --rm -p 8080:80 --name web nginx

# Request content from the running web server
curl localhost:8080

# List the running container
wslc container list

# Run an additional command inside the running container
wslc exec web cat /etc/os-release

# Stop the container
wslc container stop web
```

Because the `nginx` container was started with `--rm`, it is removed automatically once it stops.

## Build and run your own container image

To get started developing apps with `wslc.exe`, we recommend using VS Code, along with the [WSL extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-vscode-remote.remote-wsl) so you can edit your project on the Linux file system and run `wslc` commands from the integrated terminal.

Let's build a container image for an existing app project.

1. For this example, we'll use the source code from the [Hello World tutorial for Django](/windows/python/web-frameworks#hello-world-tutorial-for-django) in the Python development environment set up docs. You can skip this step if you prefer to use your own project source code. To download the HelloWorld-Django web app from GitHub, open a WSL terminal (Ubuntu for example) and enter:

    ```bash
    git clone https://github.com/<username>/helloworld-django.git
    ```

    > [!NOTE]
    > Always store your code in the same file system that you're using tools in. This will result in faster file access performance. In this example, we are using a Linux distro (Ubuntu) and want to store our project files on the WSL file system `\\wsl$`. Storing project files on the Windows file system would significantly slow things down when using Linux tools in WSL to access those files.

2. From your WSL terminal, change directories to the source code folder for this project:

    ```bash
    cd helloworld-django
    ```

3. Open the project in VS Code running on the local WSL extension server by entering:

    ```bash
    code .
    ```

    Confirm that you are connected to your WSL Linux distro by checking the green remote indicator in the bottom-left corner of your VS Code instance.

    ![VS Code WSL Remote indicator](../media/vscode-remote-indicator.png)

4. Add a `Containerfile` to the root of your project that describes how to build the image. For the Django example, a minimal `Containerfile` might look like this:

    ```dockerfile
    FROM python:3
    WORKDIR /app
    COPY requirements.txt .
    RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
    COPY . .
    EXPOSE 8000
    CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
    ```

5. From the project folder (the directory containing your `Containerfile`), build the image with `wslc build`, tagging it with a name you can reference later:

    ```powershell
    wslc build -t helloworld-django .
    ```

6. Confirm that the image was created by listing your images:

    ```powershell
    wslc image list
    ```

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Roda o agente num container.
#
#   scripts/run.sh -p "crie hello.txt" --model opencode-go/modelo
#
# O cwd entra em /workspace (bind rw) e as sessões ficam no volume nomeado.
# Credenciais entram por env, nunca por mount de ~/.pi ou ~/.config.
#
# Runtime: `DURABLE_PI_RUNTIME=docker|wslc` (padrão: auto). Em WSL, o `wslc`
# vem do Windows e não está no PATH; aponte com `DURABLE_PI_WSLC` se preciso.
set -euo pipefail

IMAGE="${DURABLE_PI_IMAGE:-durable-pi:dev}"
VOLUME="${DURABLE_PI_VOLUME:-durable-pi-home}"
RUNTIME="${DURABLE_PI_RUNTIME:-auto}"
WSLC="${DURABLE_PI_WSLC:-/mnt/c/Program Files/WSL/wslc.exe}"

if [ "$RUNTIME" = "auto" ]; then
	if command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1; then
		RUNTIME=docker
	elif [ -x "$WSLC" ]; then
		RUNTIME=wslc
	elif command -v wslc.exe >/dev/null 2>&1; then
		RUNTIME=wslc
		WSLC="$(command -v wslc.exe)"
	else
		echo "nenhum runtime de container encontrado (docker ou wslc)" >&2
		exit 1
	fi
fi

case "$RUNTIME" in
	docker) CLI=docker ;;
	wslc) CLI="$WSLC" ;;
	*)
		echo "runtime desconhecido: $RUNTIME" >&2
		exit 1
		;;
esac

if ! "$CLI" image inspect "$IMAGE" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	echo "imagem $IMAGE ausente; rode: $RUNTIME build -t $IMAGE ." >&2
	exit 1
fi

"$CLI" volume create "$VOLUME" >/dev/null
# O volume nasce root; alinha com o usuário do host para não gravar arquivos root.
"$CLI" run --rm --user 0:0 -v "$VOLUME:/home/agent" --entrypoint chown \
	"$IMAGE" -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" /home/agent >/dev/null

args=(--rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)")
if [ -t 0 ] && [ -t 1 ]; then args+=(-it); fi
args+=(-v "$PWD:/workspace" -v "$VOLUME:/home/agent" -w /workspace)
for name in DURABLE_PI_MODEL ANTHROPIC_API_KEY OPENAI_API_KEY OPENROUTER_API_KEY GOOGLE_API_KEY; do
	if [ -n "${!name:-}" ]; then args+=(-e "$name"); fi
done

exec "$CLI" run "${args[@]}" "$IMAGE" "$@"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Roda o agente num container.
#
#   scripts/run.sh -p "crie hello.txt" --model opencode-go/modelo
#
# O cwd entra em /workspace (bind rw) e as sessões ficam no volume nomeado.
# Credenciais entram por env, nunca por mount de ~/.pi ou ~/.config.
#
# Runtime e caminhos, em ordem de precedência:
#   1. variável de ambiente (DURABLE_PI_PODMAN, DURABLE_PI_WSLC, DURABLE_PI_DOCKER)
#   2. arquivo de config (DURABLE_PI_CONFIG, padrão ~/.config/durable-pi/container.conf)
#   3. PATH do sistema (e, para o wslc, o caminho padrão do Windows)
#
# Runtime: `DURABLE_PI_RUNTIME=podman|wslc|docker`; `auto` (padrão) tenta nessa
# ordem. `scripts/run.sh --runtime-info` mostra o que seria usado, sem rodar nada.
set -euo pipefail

CONFIG_FILE="${DURABLE_PI_CONFIG:-${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/durable-pi/container.conf}"
WSLC_DEFAULT="${DURABLE_PI_WSLC_DEFAULT:-/mnt/c/Program Files/WSL/wslc.exe}"

# O ambiente vence o arquivo: guarda antes de carregar e reaplica depois.
env_runtime="${DURABLE_PI_RUNTIME-}"
env_podman="${DURABLE_PI_PODMAN-}"
env_wslc="${DURABLE_PI_WSLC-}"
env_docker="${DURABLE_PI_DOCKER-}"
env_image="${DURABLE_PI_IMAGE-}"
env_volume="${DURABLE_PI_VOLUME-}"

if [ -f "$CONFIG_FILE" ]; then
	# shellcheck disable=SC1090
	. "$CONFIG_FILE"
fi
[ -n "$env_runtime" ] && DURABLE_PI_RUNTIME="$env_runtime"
[ -n "$env_podman" ] && DURABLE_PI_PODMAN="$env_podman"
[ -n "$env_wslc" ] && DURABLE_PI_WSLC="$env_wslc"
[ -n "$env_docker" ] && DURABLE_PI_DOCKER="$env_docker"
[ -n "$env_image" ] && DURABLE_PI_IMAGE="$env_image"
[ -n "$env_volume" ] && DURABLE_PI_VOLUME="$env_volume"

RUNTIME="${DURABLE_PI_RUNTIME:-auto}"
IMAGE="${DURABLE_PI_IMAGE:-durable-pi:dev}"
VOLUME="${DURABLE_PI_VOLUME:-durable-pi-home}"

# resolve_bin <caminho explícito> <nome no PATH> <fallback>
resolve_bin() {
	if [ -n "$1" ]; then
		[ -x "$1" ] && printf '%s' "$1"
		return 0
	fi
	if command -v "$2" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
		command -v "$2"
		return 0
	fi
	if [ -n "$3" ] && [ -x "$3" ]; then
		printf '%s' "$3"
	fi
	return 0
}

PODMAN_BIN="$(resolve_bin "${DURABLE_PI_PODMAN:-}" podman "")"
WSLC_BIN="$(resolve_bin "${DURABLE_PI_WSLC:-}" wslc.exe "$WSLC_DEFAULT")"
DOCKER_BIN="$(resolve_bin "${DURABLE_PI_DOCKER:-}" docker "")"

case "$RUNTIME" in
	podman)
		[ -n "$PODMAN_BIN" ] || { echo "podman não encontrado; defina DURABLE_PI_PODMAN" >&2; exit 1; }
		CLI="$PODMAN_BIN"
		;;
	wslc)
		[ -n "$WSLC_BIN" ] || { echo "wslc não encontrado; defina DURABLE_PI_WSLC" >&2; exit 1; }
		CLI="$WSLC_BIN"
		;;
	docker)
		[ -n "$DOCKER_BIN" ] || { echo "docker não encontrado; defina DURABLE_PI_DOCKER" >&2; exit 1; }
		CLI="$DOCKER_BIN"
		;;
	auto)
		if [ -n "$PODMAN_BIN" ]; then
			RUNTIME=podman; CLI="$PODMAN_BIN"
		elif [ -n "$WSLC_BIN" ]; then
			RUNTIME=wslc; CLI="$WSLC_BIN"
		elif [ -n "$DOCKER_BIN" ]; then
			RUNTIME=docker; CLI="$DOCKER_BIN"
		else
			echo "nenhum runtime encontrado (podman, wslc, docker)" >&2
			echo "defina DURABLE_PI_PODMAN, DURABLE_PI_WSLC ou DURABLE_PI_DOCKER, ou use $CONFIG_FILE" >&2
			exit 1
		fi
		;;
	*)
		echo "runtime desconhecido: $RUNTIME (use podman, wslc, docker ou auto)" >&2
		exit 1
		;;
esac

if [ "${1:-}" = "--runtime-info" ]; then
	printf 'runtime=%s\nbin=%s\nimage=%s\nvolume=%s\nconfig=%s\n' \
		"$RUNTIME" "$CLI" "$IMAGE" "$VOLUME" "$CONFIG_FILE"
	exit 0
fi

if ! "$CLI" image inspect "$IMAGE" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	echo "imagem $IMAGE ausente; rode: $RUNTIME build -t $IMAGE ." >&2
	exit 1
fi

# Idempotente: o wslc falha se o volume já existe.
"$CLI" volume create "$VOLUME" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
# O volume nasce root; alinha com o usuário do host para não gravar arquivos root.
"$CLI" run --rm --user 0:0 -v "$VOLUME:/home/agent" --entrypoint chown \
	"$IMAGE" -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" /home/agent >/dev/null

args=(--rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)")
if [ -t 0 ] && [ -t 1 ]; then args+=(-it); fi
args+=(-v "$PWD:/workspace" -v "$VOLUME:/home/agent" -w /workspace)
for name in DURABLE_PI_MODEL ANTHROPIC_API_KEY OPENAI_API_KEY OPENROUTER_API_KEY OPENCODE_API_KEY GOOGLE_API_KEY; do
	if [ -n "${!name:-}" ]; then args+=(-e "$name"); fi
done

exec "$CLI" run "${args[@]}" "$IMAGE" "$@"

# (ou aponte DURABLE_PI_CONFIG para outro caminho).

=== README trecho ===
### WSL

No WSL o runtime é o `wslc` (WSL containers, WSL ≥ 2.9.3), não há Docker no
distro. O binário fica no lado Windows:

```bash
"/mnt/c/Program Files/WSL/wslc.exe" build -t durable-pi:dev .
scripts/run.sh --help          # detecta wslc sozinho
```

`scripts/run.sh` detecta podman, wslc ou docker (`auto` tenta nessa ordem) e
aceita caminhos explícitos por variável de ambiente ou por arquivo de config,
com o ambiente vencendo o arquivo:

```bash
# ~/.config/durable-pi/container.conf  (modelo em scripts/container.conf.example)
DURABLE_PI_RUNTIME=auto
DURABLE_PI_WSLC="/mnt/c/Program Files/WSL/wslc.exe"
# DURABLE_PI_PODMAN=/usr/bin/podman
# DURABLE_PI_DOCKER=/usr/bin/docker
# DURABLE_PI_IMAGE=durable-pi:dev
# DURABLE_PI_VOLUME=durable-pi-home
```

`scripts/run.sh --runtime-info` mostra runtime, binário, imagem, volume e
caminho do config sem executar nada.

| Achado | Verificação |
|---|---|

| `requestId` novo a cada `ask()` | confirmado no código; o comentário que promete dedup está errado |
| `--session ../fora` imprime stack trace | reproduzi: `assertSessionId` lança `Error` e escapa de `main()` |
| `GOOGLE_API_KEY` não chega ao provedor | confirmado: `google.js` lê `GEMINI_API_KEY` |
| `engines` permissivo | confirmado: pi-durable exige `>=22.19.0`, nós declaramos `>=22` |
| Storage sem lock | confirmado por leitura: nada impede dois processos no mesmo arquivo |

Os quatro primeiros são bugs reais, não estilo. O do `--model` é o pior: o usuário pede um modelo, o agente usa outro silenciosamente.

Decisões, numeradas:

1. **Ordem**: corrigir o M0.1 antes do M1, ou começar o M1 e pagar depois? Recomendo corrigir antes — a TUI vai expor `/model` e `--resume`, que são exatamente os caminhos quebrados.
2. **Lock de storage**: arquivo `.lock` com `O_EXCL` + PID e detecção de lock órfão, sem dependência nova, ou `proper-lockfile` (dependência nova, precisa da sua autorização).
3. **`requestId` estável**: gravar a última submission (id + requestId + prompt) num doc da aplicação e, ao retomar, esperar a submission pendente em vez de admitir de novo. Alternativa mais simples: `--request-id` explícito no CLI.
4. **`cwd`**: gravar `agent.cwd` na criação e recusar `--continue` quando o workspace montado for outro, ou só avisar e seguir.
5. **Podman rootless**: usar `--userns=keep-id` automaticamente quando o runtime for podman, ou exigir configuração explícita.
6. **UID 0**: recusar rodar o agente como root no container, ou apenas avisar.

Se responder 1–4 eu sigo autônomo com o M0.1 em PRs separados (CLI/ciclo de vida, durabilidade de requisição, container, testes de crash).

sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use codemode to batch independent tool calls (Promise.allSettled), chain them, or filter large output, instead of many separate calls.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

<project_instructions path="/home/mjabbur/durable.pi/AGENTS.md">
# AGENTS.md

Node 24, ESM, TypeScript. `@earendil-works/pi-durable` 1.4.0, API experimental:
confira `node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-durable/dist/*.d.ts` antes de usar.
Detalhes em `docs/DURABILITY.md` e `docs/PI-CODE-MAP.md`.

## Comandos

- `npm run typecheck`, `npm run test`, `npm run lint`
- Pronto = os três verdes.

## Durabilidade (não negociável)

- Callback de commit é puro: só `tx.entry()` e `tx.doc()`. Sem I/O, rede, relógio, log.
- Efeito externo só em fase de task: grave intenção + idempotency key, chame,
  grave resultado. No resume, consulte a chave antes de repetir.
- `requestId` estável em todo submit. Entrega é ao menos uma vez.
- Estado é o que foi commitado; memória é cache.
- Determinístico entre checkpoints: `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `process.env`
  e fetch não registrados não entram em prompt nem em decisão.
- `Context` do Chord é por chamada; não guarde nem reuse após settle.
- `defineDoc` sempre com `version`, `history` e `checkpointWhen`.
- Um processo por storage. `MemoryStorage` em teste, SQLite em produção.

## Falhas

- Erro de storage encerra o Harness: escute `harness.closed`, não retente
  `commit`; reabra e reenvie com o mesmo `requestId`.
- `ConversationBusy` e `ReadAfterWrite` são fluxo normal, não bug.
- Todo `await` novo que cruza I/O exige teste de crash (matar e reabrir).

## TypeScript

- `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` ligados.
- Sem `any`; sem `as` para silenciar. Borda externa: `unknown` + schema.
- Tools via `defineTool` (TypeBox). `import type`; ESM com `.js`; sem barrel.

## Código do Pi

Mapa de componentes e ordem de leitura: `docs/PI-CODE-MAP.md`. `rg` pelo símbolo
antes de abrir arquivo. `dist/*.d.ts` é a API real da versão instalada.
Registre achados em `NOTES.md` com `path:linha`, não no chat.

## Escopo

Diff mínimo; sem refatorar fora do pedido; dependência nova: pergunte.
`PROGRESS.md` com estado, decisões e próximos passos.

</project_instructions>
